newsitem.title: UK: Thrifty British disappoint in pre-Christmas sales.
newsitem.headline: Thrifty British disappoint in pre-Christmas sales.

text.p: Mounting evidence of disappointing and patchy pre-Christmas sales suggest thrifty UK consumers remain price sensitive, dispelling fears of a return to the runaway consumer spending of the late 1980s, economists said.

But the prospect of tax cuts and building society windfalls later in the year suggests underlying consumption remains strong and will continue to be the driving force behind UK economic growth in 1997.

"It is possible that shoppers are beginning to resist attempts by high street retailers to squeeze up profit margins," said Union Plc chief economist Philip Shaw after the British Retail Consortium said retail sales growth slowed in December.
"But I would be hesitant to draw too many conclusions about one month's data, particularly if that's December or January, which should really be taken together."
The BRC December survey, released on Tuesday, was the latest anecdotal evidence to suggest retailers missed out on the pre-Christmas boom they had been counting on.

The BRC said like-for-like sales grew 4.3 percent year-on-year in value in December, the slowest rate since April. Growth was in line with that recorded last December but down from the 4.9 percent rate seen in November and 5.9 percent in October.
Schroders economist David Philpotts said the survey, along with the recent weaker than expected CBI distributive trades survey, dampened fears of a consumer-led boom in 1997.
"Although the consumer is clearly showing some momentum heading into 1997, talk of a boom is very misplaced and this may well be the start of a return to normality," he said.
Economists said the underlying trend for consumption remained robust, and they continued to expect growth of around four percent in 1997.

"The BRC survey was probably weaker than most were anticipating, but the financial position of consumers going into the start of 1997 is still very positive," said Bank America economist Jeremy Hawkins. "I suspect December was a blip around a pretty strong upward trend."

The BRC survey and trading statements from a number of retailers recently suggest spending in December was patchy with demand for consumer durables holding up fairly well but clothing and footwear sales suffering.
The BRC said spending on electrical and electronic goods continued its reasonable trend in December, adding there was no evidence of boom time conditions.

This was reflected in an upbeat trading statement from electrical retailing group Dixons Group Plc. It said sales were up eight percent in the eight weeks including Christmas, but still below market expectations for growth of around 10 percent.
Houseware sales were also reasonable in December, the BRC said, as were do-it-yourself sales on the back of the revitalised housing market.
But footwear and clothing came under pressure, despite retailers slashing prices prior to Christmas.
"Retailers have been experiencing strong demand in the clothing sector recently and have been hiking up prices. So it may well be that consumers have had enough," said Philpotts.

A gloomy report last Thursday from retail giant Sears Plc seemed to confirm flagging demand. The group said Christmas sales had been disappointing, adding annual profits would be below last year's levels.
Consumer goods and homewear retailer Argos Plc echoed these sentiments last Friday when it issued a profit warning and said sales in the second half of the year were lower than expected.
Hawkins said consumers' resistance to price rises may prompt retailers to change their pricing policies.

"It seems to be a way of life now that consumers will shop around, so there could be some change in pricing policy by retailers to accommodate that," he said, adding price hikes may be less marked and more cautious than previously.
But bargain hunting by consumers will not necessarily mean lower inflation next year, economists said.

"It's been a characteristic of the recovery since 1992 that as soon as retailers hike prices, they've had to reverse them in subsequent months," said Philpotts. "But there's still a good case that inflation may surprise on the upside next year."
Hawkins said erratic energy and food prices forced up by the cold weather may yet hit the retail price index in the near term.
